why.correct: Leading zeros never count; the trailing zero after the decimal point does. 0.00620 = 6.20 × 10⁻³, three significant figures.
options: This counts every digit, but the zeros in front of the 6 only show where the decimal point is.
This counts the zeros after the decimal point, which only place the 6.
Right: the leading zeros only place the decimal point; 6, 2 and the final 0 count.
The final zero comes after a nonzero digit and after the decimal point, so it was measured and counts.

why.correct: Milli means 10⁻³, so 2.5 ms = 2.5 × 10⁻³ s = 0.0025 s.
Multiplying or dividing: keep as many significant figures as the least precise value. 100.0 m and 12.47 s each have four, so 8.019 m/s.
options: Right: both measurements have four significant figures, so the result keeps four.
Two figures throws away precision the measurements had; both data values have four.
A calculator does not know how precise the data are; extra digits claim precision nobody measured.
One figure throws away most of the precision of four-figure data.

why.correct: Area = 1.2 m × 0.80 m = 0.96 m². Each meter is 100 cm, and a square meter is 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm², so 0.96 m² = 9600 cm² (two significant figures).
The SI base units for length, mass and time are the meter (m), the kilogram (kg) and the second (s).
options: These are older lab units. SI uses the meter and the kilogram.
SI mass is the kilogram, and SI time is the second, not the minute.
Right: m, kg and s. The kilogram is the one base unit with a prefix built in.
The kilometer and the hour are convenient but not base units; use m and s.

why.correct: Units cancel and combine like numbers: (m/s) ÷ s = m/s².
options: That would come from multiplying m/s by s, not dividing.
Right: (m/s) ÷ s = m/(s·s) = m/s², read "meters per second squared".
Dividing by seconds puts another s in the denominator, not the numerator.
This flips the whole unit; only one more second goes below the line.

why.correct: 1.5 h × (3600 s / 1 h) = 5400 s (two significant figures; 5.4 × 10³ s).
For a sum or difference, keep the fewest decimal places of the data: 12.4 m + 3.2 m = 15.6 m.
options: Adding follows decimal places, not the count of significant figures; both values are known to 0.1 m.
A second decimal place claims precision to 0.01 m that neither measurement had.
Dropping the decimal throws away the tenths both measurements had, and it also rounds the wrong way.
Right: when adding, the answer keeps the fewest decimal places of the data. Both have one decimal place.

why.correct: d = vt. Divide both sides by v: d/v = t. Units check: m ÷ (m/s) = s.
options: This flips the fraction. Check with units: (m/s) ÷ m = 1/s, not seconds.
Right: divide both sides by v, and v cancels on the right.
Multiplying by v does not undo multiplying by v; divide instead.
v multiplies t, so it is removed by dividing, not subtracting.

why.correct: Undo in reverse order: x − x₀ = vt, then v = (x − x₀)/t.
options: Right: subtract x₀ from both sides, then divide both sides by t.
Dividing first leaves x₀/t, not x₀. Undo the addition before the multiplication.
x₀ was added on the right, so it is removed by subtracting it from both sides.
The fraction is upside down; check units: s ÷ m is not m/s.

why.correct: Δ always means final minus initial: ΔT = 9.0 °C − 14.5 °C = −5.5 °C. The minus sign says the temperature went down.
Substitute with units: x = 1.20 m + (0.45 m/s)(4.0 s) = 1.20 m + 1.8 m = 3.0 m. 0.45 and 4.0 each have two significant figures.
Units check: (m/s)/m = 1/s. A time must be in s, so the expression is upside down; t = d/v gives m ÷ (m/s) = s. It also gives less time for a faster speed, as it should.
options: Right: a correct expression for a time must come out in seconds. Checking units catches upside-down fractions.
A symbolic answer is supposed to contain symbols; that is not the problem.
The question asks only for a time over a distance; x₀ is not needed.
d is in the expression; the time does depend on it, but upside down, which is the real problem.

why.correct: ρ = m/V → ρV = m → V = m/ρ. Units: kg ÷ (kg/m³) = m³.
options: This is upside down. Units: (kg/m³) ÷ kg = 1/m³, not m³.
Units: (kg/m³)(kg) = kg²/m³, not a volume.
ρ and m are joined by division, so subtraction cannot separate them (and they have different units).
Right: multiply both sides by V, then divide both sides by ρ.

why.correct: A subscript is a label. v₀ ("v naught") is the velocity at the start; v with no subscript is usually the value at a later time t.
options: v₀ can be any value; a subscript is a label, not a number to multiply or set equal.
A subscript never multiplies; it only names which value of v you mean.
Right: by convention a 0 subscript labels the initial value of the quantity.
A power is written as a superscript (v²), not a subscript.

why.correct: t = (x − x₀)/v = (9.0 m − 3.0 m) ÷ 1.5 m/s = 4.0 s. Rearrange in symbols first, then substitute once.
Write one equation per part: t₁ = d/v₁ and t₂ = d/v₂. Total time = d/v₁ + d/v₂. Units: m ÷ (m/s) = s for each term.
options: Right: each part takes distance ÷ speed, and the times add.
This treats the trip as if it ran at the plain average of the two speeds, which is only true if each speed lasts the same time.
Units: m × (m/s) is not a time. Times come from dividing distance by speed.
Units: (m/s) ÷ m = 1/s, not a time; the fraction is upside down.

why.correct: d = vt with v fixed: d ∝ t. Multiply t by 3 and d is multiplied by 3.
options: That would be true if d depended on t², but at a steady speed d = vt has t to the first power.
Right: d is directly proportional to t, so tripling t triples d.
Riding longer at the same speed covers more distance, not less.
Distance depends on time here; only the speed is held steady.
Right: t is inversely proportional to v, so multiplying v by 1.5 divides t by 1.5.
Faster means less time; v is in the denominator.
v is not squared in t = d/v, and the time should shrink, not grow.
Halving the time would need twice the speed, not 1.5 times.

why.correct: Δx ∝ t². The time is 3 times as long, so Δx is 3² = 9 times as large: 9 × 0.50 m = 4.5 m.
d = v²/(2a), a fixed: d ∝ v². Factor = 3² = 9. This is why speed matters so much for braking.
options: That treats d as proportional to v, but the speed is squared.
Squaring 3 gives 9, not 2 × 3. A square multiplies the factor by itself.
Right: d ∝ v², so 3 times the speed gives 3² = 9 times the distance.
The speed is on top of the fraction, so a larger speed gives a larger distance.

why.correct: Write the factor for each change and multiply: (2)²/(2) = 4/2 = 2.
options: The two changes do not cancel: x is squared but z is not.
Right: doubling x multiplies y by 2² = 4, and doubling z divides it by 2. 4 ÷ 2 = 2.
This counts the effect of x but forgets that z also doubled, in the denominator.
z is in the denominator, so doubling it divides y by 2 rather than multiplying.

why.correct: t = d/v, with d fixed: t ∝ 1/v. B's time = 48 s ÷ 1.5 = 32 s.
Test with a factor: if t × 2 gives Q × 4 = Q × 2², then Q ∝ t².
options: A direct proportion would only double Q when t doubles.
An inverse relationship would halve Q when t doubles.
A square root would multiply Q by about 1.41 when t doubles.
Right: a factor of 2 in t giving a factor of 4 = 2² in Q is the mark of a square relationship.

why.correct: With d fixed, t ∝ 1/v, so speeding up shortens the time and v × t stays equal to d.

variables.name: The trip time t
variables.why: t = d/v: a larger v in the denominator gives a smaller t.

variables.name: The trip length d
variables.why: The route is the same, so d is fixed by the question.

variables.name: The product v × t
variables.why: v × t = d, which stays the same: v goes up by the same factor that t goes down.

why.correct: Cost ∝ area ∝ s². Factor for s: 45/30 = 1.5. Factor for the cost: 1.5² = 2.25. Cost = 2.25 × $2.00 = $4.50.
t = d/v → vt = d. With d fixed, v and t are inversely proportional: one doubles, the other halves.
options: Right: in an inverse relationship the product of the two quantities stays constant.
This is a direct proportion; here v is in the denominator.
v is not squared, so the factor is ½, not ¼.
Fixing d is exactly what makes t depend on v alone.

why.correct: Pick two points on the best-fit line, far apart, not data points: (0 s, 1.2 m) and (10 s, 6.2 m). Slope = rise/run = (6.2 m − 1.2 m) ÷ (10 s − 0 s) = 0.50 m/s.
A slope means "change in y per change in x". Here that is meters of height per second: the rate at which the balloon rises.
options: Right: the slope is a change in height per change in time, so it is the balloon's upward speed.
Height at a moment is read straight off the graph, not from the slope.
That is a time read from the horizontal axis, not a rate.
The starting height is the vertical intercept, 1.2 m.

why.correct: For a line y = mx + b, b is the value of y at x = 0. Timing started with the balloon already 1.2 m up.
options: That is the slope, 0.50 m/s.
The gain is 6.2 m − 1.2 m = 5.0 m, a change, not the intercept.
The intercept is a real starting value: the balloon was released from a height above the ground.
Right: the intercept is the value of y when x is zero.

why.correct: Real data scatter. The first and last points here give (6.4 − 1.1) ÷ 10 = 0.53 m/s, while the best-fit line, which balances points above and below it, gives 0.50 m/s from all six measurements.
options: They are plotted; the issue is that each one carries some random error.
Any two points give a slope, but two scattered points give a less reliable one than a line fit to all six.
Right: each point has some measurement error; the best-fit line uses all the data, so its slope is more reliable.
A best-fit line usually passes between points, with about as many above as below.

why.correct: Area of the rectangle = height × width = 2.5 m/s × 14 s = 35 m. Units: (m/s)(s) = m.
Slope units = (y unit)/(x unit); area units = (y unit) × (x unit).
options: These are swapped: a slope divides the units, an area multiplies them.
The axis unit alone is neither; slope and area combine both axes' units.
Slope is y over x, not x over y, and an area multiplies y by x.
Right: slope = (m/s) ÷ s = m/s²; area = (m/s) × s = m.

why.correct: The region is a triangle: area = ½ × base × height = ½ × 4.0 s × 8.0 m/s = 16 m.
Linearize by matching y = mx: y = d, x = t², m = ½a. Then a = 2 × slope.
options: d against t curves upward because d depends on t², so it has no single slope.
Right: d = (½a)(t²) has the form y = mx with x = t², so the graph is a line through the origin with slope ½a.
The slope is the factor multiplying t², which is ½a, so a = 2 × slope, not slope = 2a.
Squaring d does not undo the square on t; this graph is not a line either.

why.correct: The slope of d against t² is ½a. So a = 2 × slope = 2 × 0.36 m/s² = 0.72 m/s².
The horizontal side is adjacent to the angle: vₓ = v cos θ = (20. m/s)(cos 30°) = 17 m/s.
North is the side opposite the 53° angle (measured from east): d(north) = d sin θ = 400 m × sin 53° = 320 m (2 significant figures; 3.2 × 10² m).
The components are the legs of a right triangle and the velocity is the hypotenuse: v = √(9.0² + 12²) = √225 = 15 m/s.
Do not memorize "x uses cosine". Find the side adjacent to the angle you are given: it gets cosine; the opposite side gets sine.
options: Cosine gives the side adjacent to θ, which here is the vertical side.
Tangent is a ratio of the two legs, not a leg divided by the hypotenuse.
Right: measured from the vertical, the horizontal side is opposite θ, so it uses sine.
A component is shorter than the vector; dividing by cos θ makes it longer.

why.correct: Physics 1 angles are in degrees. Set the calculator to degree mode before any trig: cos 60° = 0.500.
options: Cosine is positive for angles from 0° to 90°.
Right: it read 60 in another angle unit and gave −0.952. In degree mode, cos 60° = 0.500.
Changing the function does not fix a calculator in the wrong angle mode.
Angles in degrees are entered as written; the mode is the problem.

why.correct: tan θ = opposite/adjacent = v<sub>y</sub>/vₓ = 5.0/12, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.417) = 23°.
Tip to tail: draw the second vector starting at the tip of the first; the resultant goes from the first tail to the last tip. Here it is a 3-4-5 triangle.
options: Perpendicular displacements do not add as plain numbers; 7.0 m is the distance walked.
Subtracting works only for vectors along the same line in opposite directions.
The resultant points from the start to the end, which is north of east, not due north.
Right: the two legs are perpendicular, so the resultant is the hypotenuse √(3.0² + 4.0²) = 5.0 m, pointing between east and north.

why.correct: Add the south components: leg 1 gives 240 km × sin 37.0° = 144.4 km south; leg 2 gives 100. km south. Total = 244 km.
vₓ = v cos θ and v<sub>y</sub> = v sin θ. As θ rises, sin θ rises and cos θ falls; vₓ² + v<sub>y</sub>² stays v².
options: The magnitude is fixed, so one component can grow only if the other shrinks.
Right: v sin θ grows and v cos θ shrinks as θ increases toward 90°.
That happens when the angle decreases toward 0°.
The speed fixes the hypotenuse, but the angle decides how it splits between the legs.

why.correct: The ramp is the hypotenuse; its height is the side opposite the 25° angle: h = (3.0 m) sin 25° = 1.3 m.
